item.content:encoded:
Scout-Love Bigg Boss Controversy Raises A Big Question: Where Do You Draw The Line With Other Women?
Can you call another woman your sister and still make your girlfriend uncomfortable? Scout and Love Gill's Bigg Boss controversy puts relationship boundaries to the test.
Got Question about the News?
If your social media feed has been flooded with clips of ScoutOP and Love Gill getting rather comfortable inside the Bigg Boss 20 house, you are hardly alone. From Scout massaging Love’s feet to their physical closeness beneath a blanket, and hugs in which Love pulls Scout close, with his face pressed against her chest, their interactions have become fodder for online debate. And through it all, there is one explanation: they share a bhai-behen bond.
But here is the question: when you are in a committed relationship, does calling another woman your sister make every display of physical affection acceptable?

The controversy has struck a nerve because it is not about whether men and women can be friends. Of course they can. It is about the kind of physical familiarity a man chooses to share with another woman when he already has a girlfriend. And when those moments unfold on national television, with his partner watching alongside everyone else, the question of consideration becomes difficult to ignore.
The conversation gained momentum after Bigg Boss 20 host Rohit Shetty questioned Scout and Love’s physical closeness during Weekend Ka Vaar. Scout defended his behaviour, while Love maintained that she considered him a brother. Scout’s girlfriend, Kaashvi Hiranandani, also expressed discomfort with their equation, bringing relationship boundaries into sharper focus.
Social media has since been awash with opinions about whether their interactions cross a line. But beneath the noise lies a more pertinent question: should your partner have to explain why certain kinds of physical intimacy with another woman make them uncomfortable?
The ‘She’s Like My Sister’ Defence Can Only Go So Far
Having female friends is not a betrayal. Hugging a friend, sharing a joke or offering comfort does not automatically threaten a relationship. But there is a difference between having a friendship and being so physically familiar with someone that the nature of that closeness becomes a talking point, particularly when you are already committed to somebody else.
Foot massages, getting physically close beneath a blanket and hugs that involve this degree of bodily familiarity are hardly what most people would associate with a conventional sibling-like equation. And when these moments are playing out on national television, it becomes difficult to understand why the bhai-behen label is being treated as an all-purpose explanation. At some point, the question has to be asked: if the relationship is so unequivocally sibling-like, why does the physical intimacy look so at odds with the way they describe it?
The problem with hiding behind the bhai-behen defence is that a label cannot automatically sanitise every kind of physical contact. Calling a woman your sister does not make every gesture appropriate by default, particularly when you have a girlfriend who is watching these interactions unfold in front of an entire nation. Friendship is one thing; repeatedly engaging in this degree of physical familiarity is quite another. And a committed relationship demands enough awareness to recognise that distinction.
The question isn’t whether Scout and Love are entitled to define their bond as sibling-like. It’s whether Scout believes that calling her his sister absolves him of any responsibility to consider how his behaviour reflects on his relationship with Kaashvi. Because being committed to someone should mean more than insisting that your intentions are innocent. It should also mean knowing when your behaviour is inappropriate for the relationship you are in.
Your Girlfriend Shouldn’t Have To Watch The Internet Tell Her What To Think
Perhaps the most uncomfortable aspect of the controversy is the position in which Kaashvi finds herself. Her boyfriend’s interactions with another woman are playing out on national television, being clipped, circulated and dissected by strangers, while she is left to contend with the public conversation around them.
You may trust your partner’s intentions, but that does not mean you are obliged to feel comfortable with every interaction.
And this is where the argument that nothing happened falls short. A relationship is not simply about avoiding infidelity. It is also about the everyday choices that demonstrate consideration for the person you are with.
A committed man should be capable of recognising that not every form of physical familiarity is worth defending simply because he believes it is innocent. There is a difference between maintaining a friendship and engaging in behaviour that could reasonably make your partner question where she stands.
That is not about seeking permission to interact with women. It is about exercising the judgement that commitment demands.
Being Committed Means Knowing When To Draw The Line
One of the laziest arguments in these situations is that a partner who objects to physical closeness with another woman must be jealous or controlling. Sometimes, jealousy can become unreasonable. But not every objection to a partner’s behaviour is an attempt to control them.
There is a difference between demanding that your boyfriend stop speaking to women and expecting him to exercise discretion about physical intimacy. There is also a difference between policing a friendship and asking whether certain interactions are appropriate for someone who is already in a committed relationship.
And the standard should work both ways. If a man would be uncomfortable watching his girlfriend share the same degree of physical intimacy with another man, it is worth asking why he would expect her to accept it from him. Commitment cannot mean one set of rules for yourself and another for your partner.
The responsibility also lies with the person in the relationship, not the other woman alone. Love should not be made the villain simply because she is part of the footage being discussed. Scout is responsible for the commitments he has made, just as Kaashvi is entitled to express what she finds acceptable within their relationship.
Respect Is About More Than Staying Faithful
There is a tendency to reduce relationship loyalty to one question: did you cheat or did you not? But fidelity is not the only measure of how someone treats their partner.
You can insist that an interaction was innocent and still fail to appreciate why it hurt someone. You can have no romantic interest in another woman and still be careless about the boundaries of your own relationship. And you can defend your freedom to behave as you please while overlooking the fact that commitment involves responsibilities, not just privileges.
This does not mean a man in a relationship must avoid every hug or affectionate exchange with a female friend. It means he should understand the difference between ordinary friendship and a level of physical familiarity that warrants a conversation with his partner, especially when he might struggle to accept the same behaviour in reverse.
Ultimately, the controversy raises a question worth confronting: is it enough to insist that you meant no harm, or does being a good partner also require you to recognise when your behaviour disrespects the relationship you are in?
You can call another woman your sister. You can insist that the relationship is platonic. But when you have a girlfriend, the question is not merely what you think your behaviour means. It is whether you are showing the consideration, judgement and respect that your own relationship deserves.
Quick Answers
The controversy sparked widespread online debate due to ScoutOP and Love Gill's close physical interactions inside the Bigg Boss 20 house, including foot massages, sharing blankets, and tight hugs, despite Scout having a girlfriend outside the show.
